newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD says too early to predict on EMU target.
newsitem.headline: German SPD says too early to predict on EMU target.

text.p: The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) said on Friday it was too early to say if Germany would achieve a 1997 budget deficit of 3.0 percent of economic output.
"We can't judge this at the current time," SPD finance spokeswoman Ingrid Matthaeus-Maier told a news conference.

Matthaeus-Maier, responding to Finance Minister Theo Waigel's budget plans for the rest of this year and 1998, said the government was making savings in the wrong places and doing nothing to fight record unemployment.
Waigel had told reporters Germany would have a deficit of 3.0 percent of gross domestic product, thus qualifying for Europe's single currency.
Matthaeus-Maier said it was right to aim for participation in monetary union but added the three percent target in the Maastricht Treaty did not have to be interpreted as 3.0.
"If the mark can be stable with 3.1 percent, then the euro can as well," she said.
Matthaeus-Maier said she had doubts about whether Waigel's supplementary budget for 1997 conformed to the constitution.
The extra budget puts borrowing above investment for the year -- a situation the constitution only allows in the case of economic imbalance.

Several economists have said this is only permissible if the higher borrowing is used to fight the cause of the imbalance -- in this case, high unemployment -- and that they see little evidence of this in Waigel's plans.

"I have my doubts about whether what Waigel is doing conforms to the constitution because he's only filling holes in the budget," Matthaeus-Maier said. But she added the party had no plans to complain to the Federal Constitutional Court.
She said Waigel's decision to increase the deficit this year and suspend some debt repayments next year meant he was increasing the burden future generations would have to pay.
